title: Real-Factory Credentials From Customs Shipping Records
one_liner: Turn public US import records into supplier-owned reputation credentials and audit-ready reasonable-care dossiers that prove a factory is a real manufacturer.
customer: Small and mid-size US importers of record (Amazon and Shopify brands, furniture, hardware and apparel distributors) re-sourcing to Vietnam, India, Mexico and Turkey. Customs brokers are a channel, and factories are the second payer.
problem: The importer of record is investigated first, and liability turns on whether it exercised reasonable care about the supplier's origin claims. In August 2026 the White House published a report on transshipment, a 40% penalty tariff applies, and CBP has expanded inspections of shipments from Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Mexico. Small importers cannot tell a real factory from a trading company or a re-labeller, and sourcing agents' claims are unverifiable.
solution: Supplier Proof. Build a profile per factory from three or more years of US import records (shipper and consignee names, volumes, product codes, ports, cadence) plus corporate registry and location data, flag anomalies such as volume beyond plausible capacity, mismatched product codes or shell-company addresses, and add optional local inspector visits. Factories claim and verify their profile and can consent to name repeat buyers as references. The output is a dossier the importer can hand to a broker or to CBP.
why_now: Tariff enforcement moved in 2025-26 from headline rates to origin verification, and the August 2026 transshipment report has put importer liability on every compliance officer's desk. Sourcing shifts away from China are happening now, so millions of dollars of orders are going to unfamiliar factories.
revenue_model: Importer subscriptions of $149-499 per month, $150-400 per dossier, inspector visits passed through at a margin, and $600-1,200 per year from factories for a verified credential once importers demand it.
non_obvious_insight: Import records are the only unforgeable cross-border reputation ledger for factories, but they are sold as raw rows to analysts. Repackaged as supplier-owned credentials with a reasonable-care wrapper, a data product becomes a compliance product with a real budget line: avoiding a 40% penalty.
first_30_days: Buy 12 months of import records for two categories (for example furniture and hardware from Vietnam and India). Auto-build about 1,000 factory profiles and hand-audit 20. Send 200 emails to sourcing managers and customs brokers. Sell the first 10 dossiers at $250 each and use them to refine the scoring.

title: Turn Foreman Paper Sign-In Sheets Into Court-Ready Records
one_liner: Foremen text a photo of the daily paper sign-in sheet, and the system timestamps it, flags overtime, break and travel-time errors, and builds an audit-ready record. The crew changes nothing.
customer: Trade subcontractors with 5 to 50 field employees (electrical, framing, concrete, HVAC, roofing) that still use paper sheets or Excel. It is sold through construction-focused insurance agents, payroll providers and construction CPAs.
problem: Most contractor wage-hour violations are recordkeeping failures: overtime miscalculations, uncompensated travel time and undocumented breaks. Paper sheets and foreman memory have no audit trail, so when a wage claim lands up to two years later the employer cannot prove what it paid. A $50,000 overtime dispute can double with liquidated damages before attorney fees. Owners don't buy time-tracking software for compliance, because compliance is not what they think they are buying.
solution: A phone number or WhatsApp thread. The foreman photographs the day's sign-in sheet, and the service extracts hours per worker, adds a trusted timestamp, and stores the original image in an append-only log with a chain-of-custody hash. Each week it reconciles hours against the payroll export (CSV from ADP, Gusto or QuickBooks Payroll) and flags mismatches: overtime not paid, drive time between sites, missing breaks, and prevailing-wage or certified-payroll classification gaps. When a claim or audit arrives, one click produces a records package with an affidavit-ready custodian statement. Insurance partners can offer it as a loss-control benefit on wage-and-hour or EPLI coverage.
why_now: Construction Dive ran this as a July 2026 compliance story. DOL Wage and Hour recovered more than $259 million in back wages for nearly 177,000 workers in fiscal 2025, and construction alone saw about 3,000 investigations and $36 million recovered for 21,000 workers. The labor squeeze, with job openings rising for a third month, keeps overtime and crew-hopping high. Photo capture, OCR and trusted timestamping are now cheap enough to deliver this for about $100 a month.
revenue_model: $99 to $299 per month per contractor by headcount; a $750 audit-response records package; a 15 to 20% recurring rebate to insurance agents or payroll partners who resell. Later add payroll-error recovery reports as a paid add-on.
non_obvious_insight: Apps like time clocks fail because crews resist changing habits, and buyers don't feel compliance risk. So sell defensibility on top of the existing paper behavior instead of replacing it. Evidence: a survey of 180 mid-market contractors found only 4% cited compliance as a concern with time tracking, and 72% who tracked time on paper or spreadsheets 'never raised a compliance concern once in the conversation'. The article notes the records 'can't answer the question' when disputes arise two years later, and cites $259M in DOL back wages and $36M recovered from construction in a single year (https://www.constructiondive.com/news/inaccurate-time-records-contractor-compliance-liability/825438/). The same Construction Dive labor page shows the squeeze (https://www.constructiondive.com/topic/labor/).
first_30_days: Week 1: recruit 5 contractors via a construction CPA or insurance agent friend, and build the intake as a shared phone number plus a spreadsheet and an OCR script. Weeks 2 to 3: run their real sign-in sheets through it, deliver a weekly variance report, and show each owner one specific overtime or drive-time gap. Week 4: charge $149 per month, and present the results to two construction insurance agencies as a loss-control add-on. Target: 8 paying contractors and 1 signed agency partner.

title: Fill-Level Sensors for Remote Vault Toilets
one_liner: Satellite-capable fill-level and usage sensors for the vault toilets on public land and in campgrounds, so pump trucks go where and when they are actually needed.
customer: Campground and recreation concessionaires operating on federal and state land, state park systems, county park departments, ski areas and trailhead managers. Second wave: event, construction and portable-restroom fleets. Pumping contractors are channel partners.
problem: Vault toilets are pumped on fixed calendars or when a hiker reports an overflow. Busy sites need pumping weekly or monthly in peak season and remote sites once every year or two. Trucks drive one to three hours each way. A full toilet closes a site, damages the visitor experience, and holiday weekends generate emergency call-outs at premium rates.
solution: An ultrasonic or time-of-flight sensor puck under the riser lid plus a PIR visit counter, on LTE-M with a narrowband satellite (NB-NTN) fallback for no-coverage sites. The dashboard forecasts 'days to full' from usage and holiday and weather calendars, then auto-generates work orders to the nearest contractor with route batching. Usage counts also drive restocking of toilet paper and cleaning visits.
why_now: Narrowband satellite IoT modules and plans have reached commercial availability, cutting the cost of monitoring a toilet 40 miles from cell coverage. Recreation agencies and concessionaires face tight staffing and budgets, so triaging truck rolls has real value.
revenue_model: USD 12-20 per toilet per month including a leased sensor (about USD 150 hardware cost). A 600-toilet concessionaire is about USD 100k per year. Route-optimization module for pumpers. Event-fleet pricing per unit per event.
non_obvious_insight: The savings isn't fewer pump-outs; it's knowing which toilets are near-full before a holiday weekend and avoiding closures and emergency call-outs. Pumpers earn per visit, so pitch them a route-density and demand-forecast tool that grows their business rather than threatening it.
first_30_days: Build 30 units from off-the-shelf modules. Pilot 5-10 toilets each with three concessionaires and two county park departments. Use the shoulder season (hunting and early winter trailheads) to test. Recruit one septic pumping company as a co-pilot partner. Convert to annual contracts before next spring's opening.

title: Fill the Empty EU Wallet: Payroll Attestations
one_liner: Issue consented, selectively disclosed employment-and-income attestations from payroll systems into EU Digital Identity Wallets, sold per verification to rental platforms, lenders and landlords fighting AI-forged payslips.
customer: Relying parties: rental and housing platforms, property managers and letting agents, consumer lenders, car-lease and telecom-contract sellers, paying EUR 0.50-3 per verified income or employment check. The issuing side is payroll providers and mid-size employers, who get a revenue share.
problem: Every member state must offer a wallet by 24 Dec 2026, and banks, telecoms and large platforms must accept it by late 2027. But a wallet holding only an ID card is a dud. The credentials people actually need to prove (income, employment, licences, tenancy history) sit in payroll and HR systems with no issuing channel. Meanwhile generative AI makes forged payslips and employment letters trivial, and landlords and lenders either eat fraud or manually call employers.
solution: An attestation issuance gateway that plugs into payroll platforms and APIs. After employee consent it issues short-lived, signed 'employment status and income band' attestations, using a qualified trust service provider partner for qualified status. Selective disclosure proves 'net income at least 3x rent' without revealing salary. A relying-party SDK and REST API handle verification. Start in rental applications in one market with acute fraud pain, such as the Netherlands, Germany or Spain. Before wallets go live, sell the same check as a QR-verifiable signed document.
why_now: The 24 Dec 2026 wallet deadline and late-2027 acceptance mandates create a supply gap. QEAA implementing rules exist. Generative forgery has collapsed trust in PDFs, and payroll vendors do not want to build issuance and carry the liability.
revenue_model: Per-verification fees of EUR 0.50-3 from relying parties, with 30% shared with the payroll provider. A white-label issuer licence for large payroll and HR vendors, and monthly minimums for landlord groups and lenders.
non_obvious_insight: Wallet adoption will be decided by which credentials are in it on day one, not by the wallet app. The two parties who want the wallet most, landlords and lenders, mainly need one credential (income) that lives in a system nobody has plugged in. Selective disclosure lets payroll data be monetized without exposing it, and the scarce asset is the issuer supply side.
first_30_days: Sign LOIs with two payroll providers (one small regional) and one rental platform or property manager group. Build a proof of concept against the EU reference wallet and a test QTSP. In parallel run a manual pre-wallet pilot where consenting employees get payroll-signed QR-verifiable income statements, so revenue starts before the wallet launches.

title: Co-op Ledger Signals: Farm Distress Early Warning
one_liner: Benchmark co-ops on their own receivables, then sell the anonymized, county-level 'who is paying whom first' data to lenders, insurers and equipment financiers as a leading indicator of farm distress.
customer: First payers: co-op managers and CFOs, who buy the benchmark dashboard. Data buyers: Farmer Mac, Farm Credit institutions, regional ag banks, equipment captive finance arms, input manufacturers, ag reinsurers and funds trading farm-exposed equities.
problem: Ag bank delinquency stats and Fed surveys lag reality by two to three quarters. Meanwhile every co-op ERP quietly holds the earliest signal: accounts-receivable aging by customer, the timing of input payments, and who is asking for deferred-payment or extended-terms deals. Farmers in trouble pay in a predictable order (operating lender, landlord, seed, then the co-op), so slow co-op payments show up long before defaults. Each co-op sees only its own trade area and cannot tell whether its collection problems are local or systemic.
solution: Ship a free-to-cheap benchmark: connect the co-op's grain and ag-retail accounting system (Agvance, Agris and similar) and get peer comparisons on A/R over 90 days, prepay behavior, and credit-line usage. In return, contribute anonymized data to a pooled index with strict privacy rules (a minimum of 5 co-ops per cell, county-by-month, no farmer-level data). Sell the county-level Farm Payment Stress Index to lenders and funds, with a second SKU for weekly harvest-pace and grain-quality metrics (moisture, test weight, damage) from scale tickets. Co-ops receive a revenue share.
why_now: Chapter 12 filings are up sharply, the Chicago Fed reports rising loan rollovers and falling cash rents, and USDA projects record farm debt. Federal data proved brittle during the fall 2025 shutdown, and lenders and funds want independent ground truth without waiting for quarterly surveys.
revenue_model: Co-op benchmark subscription ($300 to $800 a month). Index licenses to lenders and reinsurers ($25k to $150k a year). Fund data feeds ($5k to $15k a month). Co-ops receive 40% to 50% of data revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The co-op's boring back-office ledger is the best real-time farm-distress sensor in America. Co-op managers think the data is too mundane to sell. The way to get it is to give them the peer benchmark they have always wanted and only then aggregate.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 to 8 co-ops through state co-op councils and CFO peer groups with a free 'A/R health check'. Build an ETL for the two or three most common co-op ERPs. Produce the first county-level index by Q4 2026. Pitch two ag lenders and one reinsurer for paid pilots.

title: Amps Not Acres: Power Headroom for Retrofits
one_liner: Headroom reports and a load-sequencing kit that let plants add machines inside existing walls without a new transformer.
customer: Owners and plant managers of 20-300 employee manufacturers, and machine-tool, compressor and robot dealers who need to know whether a customer can power what they sell.
problem: Site selectors and economic developers think reshoring is limited by land, buildings and permits. The data say otherwise. Factory construction is down 22-32% from peak, yet nondefense capital-goods orders hit a record $85.9B in July, so equipment is going into old buildings. Transformer and switchgear prices are up 89-96% since 2019 as data centers compete for the same gear. Utility service upgrades cost six figures and take a year or more.
solution: Step 1 is a Headroom Report. It pulls 12 months of utility interval data (Green Button) and uses measured demand (NEC 220.87 allows this) to show how many kW can be added, ready for a PE stamp. Step 2 is a clamp-on CT and PLC/gateway kit that staggers compressors, furnaces, welders and spindle start-ups to cap demand peaks. Step 3 adds an optional battery or thermal-storage partner for the residual gap.
why_now: Record capital-goods orders with $953B unfilled, prices for electrical gear up sharply, and reshoring that is happening in existing buildings. No incumbent sells 'create amps in software' to a 50-person shop.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k per report (dealers pay to close sales). $5-15k for hardware and install. $200-400 a month for monitoring. Referral fees from dealers and battery vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Nameplate capacity is not the constraint. Measured coincident peak is, and it is usually far below service rating. The scarce input is amps, and amps can be created by sequencing loads.
first_30_days: Pitch 10 machine dealers on the report as a free pre-sale add-on. Get interval data from 5 plants. Partner with a licensed PE for stamping. Assemble the first controller from off-the-shelf CTs and a PLC.

title: Data Act Access-Request Desk for Independent Repairers
one_liner: A clearinghouse that files, tracks and escalates EU Data Act data-access requests to connected-product makers on behalf of independent garages, installers and fleet operators.
customer: Independent repair-shop networks, heat-pump and solar installers, agricultural-machinery service firms and small fleet operators (10-500 vehicles or machines) in the EU, plus their trade associations.
problem: Connected products must give users direct data access by design from 12 Sep 2026, and users can direct sharing to third parties. Every manufacturer will build its own portal, format and terms, and has every incentive to slow-walk independents. The EU repair directive transposition deadline (31 Jul 2026) also just passed. Small firms know wrenches, not statutory request letters or how to reach a national competent authority.
solution: A standardized request generator, a directory of each manufacturer's access method, a tracker with statutory-timeline reminders, normalization of the most-wanted data (fault codes, usage, battery health) and an escalation pack for the national authority. Launch with five manufacturers in two product categories.
why_now: The Data Act design obligation date was 12 Sep 2026, the repair directive deadline was 31 Jul 2026 and the EU repair platform is due 1 Jan 2028. Independents just received rights with no plumbing.
revenue_model: $49-149/month per shop, $5-20 per vehicle or machine per year for fleets, association licenses, and paid negotiation of bulk access terms.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance startups sell to the obligated party. The Data Act creates a beneficiary class that is fragmented and unsophisticated about law. The AirHelp pattern applies: rights that are costly to file individually but cheap to file collectively.
first_30_days: Sign two trade associations (independent aftermarket or agricultural repair). Send 20 manual requests across five OEMs and log response times, then publish an 'OEM Data Act responsiveness scorecard' to earn press and members. Charge $99/month.

title: Fire-Season Vaults for Fandom Collectors
one_liner: Red-Flag-Warning-triggered pickup and insured off-site storage for graded cards, comics, sealed games and memorabilia kept in wildfire-zone homes.
customer: Collectors holding $50K-$2M of graded trading cards, comics, sealed games and signed memorabilia in wildfire-zone ZIPs or on last-resort plans such as the California FAIR Plan (696,562 policies in June 2026).
problem: A closet of graded cards can be worth more than the contents limit on a distressed-market homeowners policy. Collectibles are usually capped or need scheduling, which retreating carriers avoid. Evacuations give minutes. Vaults exist, but storage is a one-time decision with no urgency trigger, and nobody sells 'fire season' as a product.
solution: Three steps. (1) Photograph and catalog the collection with a card-scanning app and a live price feed, producing a claim-ready inventory. (2) From June to November, the top slice of value moves to a bonded vault under agreed-value cover from a specialty coverholder. (3) The remainder goes in a pre-tagged go-case, and on a Red Flag Warning or evacuation warning within N miles a bonded courier collects it within 4 hours, or the owner drops it at a partner card shop. Everything is returned in December.
why_now: The trading-card boom (Pokemon at 85B+ cards, a $28M Kickstarter TCG, blind-box resale above RMB 1,000 with VCs funding the resale layer) has turned closets into six-figure assets. FAIR Plan exposure hit $768B (secondary source) with a 29.1% rate hike. New carriers expanding under California's Sustainable Insurance Strategy have said nothing about scheduled personal property.
revenue_model: Annual fee of about 0.6-1.2% of stored declared value (storage plus insurance), a $150-400 courier trigger fee per activation, and commission on the agreed-value policy. An average $250K customer is worth about $2.5K a year.
non_obvious_insight: Insurers are retreating from the house, not from the objects. Fandom wealth is small, portable and already authenticated (slab cert numbers), so it is the one wildfire-zone asset you can move in a single trip and value without an adjuster. The business is logistics plus underwriting data, not a vault.
first_30_days: Pre-sell 30 founding memberships through Discord, Reddit and 10 card and comic shops in fire-prone ZIPs (Altadena, Topanga, Santa Rosa, Boulder foothills). Partner with an existing vault and a Lloyd's coverholder rather than building either. Run the first live drill when Santa Ana wind season starts in October-November.

title: Unwind Desk for California's 3-Day Car Return
one_liner: A per-return concierge that unwinds a cancelled used-car deal (lender, add-on administrators, DMV, sales tax, commissions) inside California's new 48-hour refund deadline. It then turns the return data into a return-risk pool.
customer: California used-car dealers, especially independents and BHPH lots that sell 30 to 200 used cars a month and have no back-office bench. They pay $195 to $250 per return, or a standby retainer. Later, insurers and MGAs buy the underwriting data.
problem: From Oct 1, 2026, SB 766 gives buyers a 3-day right to cancel a used vehicle priced at $50,000 or less. Within 48 hours of cancellation the dealer must cancel the contract and refund the buyer, less only the deductions the law allows for mileage and damage. That is easy to write and very hard to do. The cost of an unwind is the cascade, not the car. The dealer has to reach the lender that has funded or is holding the contract, cancel each service contract and GAP with its administrator, and charge back the F&I commission. It also has to reverse the title, registration and sales tax, refund the down payment and any trade, and document the vehicle condition to justify any deduction. Independents have never done this at volume, and one botched unwind creates a refund violation and a private-plaintiff claim.
solution: Unwind-as-a-service. The dealer forwards the cancellation notice. The desk runs a checklist workflow that notifies the lender, submits cancellations to administrators with the correct pro-rata or full-refund basis, prepares the DMV and tax reversals, calculates the refund and permitted deductions, and produces a compliance file that meets the two-year retention rule. A delivery-day photo and video capture link is bundled, because permitted deductions depend on condition documentation. After 6 months of volume, the desk holds the only dataset on return rates, timing and loss per return in a mandatory-return regime. That data is enough to price a per-unit return-risk cover (roughly $60 to $120 per used unit) through a licensed MGA or insurer partner.
why_now: The law takes effect Oct 1, 2026, so the first returns arrive within days. No US state has had a mandatory 3-day return on used cars at this scale. The 2025 to 2026 run of subprime stress, roughly 30% of trade-ins underwater and repossessions at about 3M a year, means many buyers will discover mid-week that they can't afford the payment. That is the buyer most likely to use the cancellation right.
revenue_model: Flat fee per processed return ($195 to $250). Standby retainer of about $99 per month per store for priority handling. Phase 2: 10 to 20% of premium as an MGA on the return-risk pool. Phase 3: license the cancellation-cascade workflow to DMS and eContract vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody knows the real return rate. Everyone models it on Carvana's 7-day return, but the buyers who return are not typical, because the F&I office sees payment shock and buyer's remorse first. A 48-hour refund deadline is shorter than the time a lender, administrator or DMV normally takes to process anything, so the dealer's exposure is process failure, not vehicle depreciation. Whoever owns the process owns the data, and the data is what makes the insurance product priceable.
first_30_days: Write the cascade checklist by state and by lender for the 20 most common California indirect lenders and 15 administrators. Approach the California Independent Automobile Dealers Association and 10 high-volume independents. Sell a $99 per month standby plan with a guaranteed 24-hour turnaround per return. Handle the first 20 returns manually with a shared spreadsheet and e-sign before writing any software. Log every step's time and dollar cost, since that log becomes the actuarial dataset.

title: Year-Three Warranty Claims Agent and Failure Index
one_liner: An agent that files manufacturer, retailer and credit-card extended-warranty claims when your stuff dies, paid on success, whose claims data becomes a durability index that Amazon's star ratings cannot provide.
customer: Consumers who bought $200 to $3,000 durables (appliances, e-bikes, laptops, mattresses, power tools) in the past 1 to 4 years. Later data buyers: home-warranty and insurance firms, retailers, brand quality teams and AI shopping agents.
problem: Amazon's incentives end at the return window, and reviews freeze at week two, but failures happen in year two to four. The money left behind sits in three layers: manufacturer warranties, retailer protection plans and credit-card extended warranty. It goes unclaimed because people cannot find the receipt, do not know which layer applies, or quit at the phone tree. Meanwhile shoppers have no independent durability signal, and the one consumer tool for spotting fake reviews, Fakespot, was shut down by Mozilla in July 2025 for lack of a business model.
solution: The consumer connects a receipt source (read-only, receipts only, opt-in) and the agent builds a coverage ledger for big purchases: warranty end dates, card-benefit eligibility, retailer plan status. When the user texts that the dishwasher died, the agent assembles the claim packet (receipt, serial number, photos, symptom), files with the right layer over email, chat or a voice agent, and chases it to resolution. Every outcome (brand, model, failure mode, age at failure) goes into an anonymized Failure Index.
why_now: LLM agents can now read messy receipts and run multi-channel claims at a cost per claim low enough for a success-fee model. AI shopping assistants and agentic checkout need trustworthy durability signals, which star ratings do not supply. Fakespot's 2025 shutdown proved consumers will not pay to check reviews, so the payer has to be the claim recovery itself.
revenue_model: A success fee of 20% to 25% of recovered value (refund, repair or replacement), or $19 flat per filed claim. In year two, license the Failure Index by API or report to warranty administrators, insurers, retailers and shopping agents ($2k to $25k per month). Affiliate referrals for a better replacement at the moment of failure.
non_obvious_insight: The unowned moment in commerce is month 25, not the purchase. Every incumbent (Amazon, brands, card issuers) profits when claiming is hard, and a failure someone bothered to claim is a labeled ground-truth data point, unlike a star rating. Sell claims recovery to consumers, who will pay, and the byproduct dataset is what the institutions that price durability will pay for.
first_30_days: Run it concierge-style. Put up a landing page: 'Did your appliance, e-bike or laptop die within 3 years? We file the claim, you pay only if we recover.' Recruit 30 claimants from Reddit (r/appliances, r/ebikes) and local Facebook groups. Draft claims with an LLM and send them by hand, logging every outcome. Pick one category (for example e-bike batteries or robot vacuums) and publish five public posts on what the claims data shows. Approach one home-warranty or appliance-retail company for a paid data pilot.

title: A Price Index and Exchange for Agent Labor
one_liner: Publish the going rate and accuracy for standardized agent-delivered tasks (per 1,000 invoices, per verified ticket resolution), then let buyers run reverse auctions against it.
customer: CFOs, procurement and ops leaders at enterprises buying agent services, investors and analysts, and later the agent vendors that bid for work.
problem: Buyers have no reference price. Vendor pricing is opaque and shifting from seats to outcomes, quality varies widely, and Gartner says only about 130 of thousands of 'agentic' vendors are real. Unit token prices fell about 67% but bills rose, so nobody knows what a task should cost.
solution: Define standardized task classes with public test sets and acceptance criteria (invoice extraction and coding, tier-1 support resolution, KYC document review, meeting scheduling). Run blinded monthly bake-offs across vendors on hidden holdouts and publish a quality and cost-per-verified-outcome index. Sell buyer-side bake-offs on customers' own data. Later add an RFQ exchange with escrow released when acceptance tests pass.
why_now: Outcome pricing arrived in 2026, agent-washing is rampant, and benchmarks exist for models but not end-to-end vendors. Project Vend-style real-world evaluations show that outcomes need checklists and supervision to be trustworthy.
revenue_model: $20-$60k/year subscriptions for enterprises and investors, $15-$40k custom bake-offs, and a 3-5% exchange take rate later.
non_obvious_insight: Markets need a benchmark price before they need a marketplace, as freight and housing indices came first. Agent labor has large quality and price dispersion, and the party that publishes the reference sets the negotiation frame for the whole category.
first_30_days: Pick 2 task classes and assemble public plus holdout data. Run 6 vendors and publish the first index free with full methodology. Sell the first custom bake-off to a buyer and use it as a case study.

title: Cure Desk: Medical-Bill Triage for Delinquent Tenants
one_liner: A landlord-paid service that turns a late-rent notice into a medical-bill rescue, using hospital charity care, bill negotiation and coverage re-enrollment to free up the cash that pays the rent.
customer: Multifamily and single-family-rental operators (500-20,000 units) pay per cured account.
problem: 20% of renter households paid late or missed rent in 2025, and middle-income households jumped from 14.3% to 21.6%. About 4.8M people lost coverage after enhanced ACA subsidies expired. Landlords now face AI-assisted pro se tenant filings (41,000+ federal pro se cases in 2025) and increasingly conclude that cash-for-keys is cheaper than winning an eviction.
solution: When a resident is 3-5 days late, the property manager sends an opt-in text. If medical bills or a coverage loss are the cause, an advocate applies to the hospital's financial-assistance program (nonprofit hospitals must have one), negotiates the bill, sets payment plans and opens a special enrollment period. The landlord pays a success fee (roughly $300-500) only when arrears are cured, versus thousands per eviction.
why_now: Subsidy expiry created millions of self-pay patients in 2026, delinquency is at series highs, and the legal cost of eviction is rising with AI-generated filings. Medicaid churn from Jan 2027 will add more.
revenue_model: Success fee per cured account, with an optional $/unit/month retainer for early-warning outreach.
non_obvious_insight: A missed rent payment is the earliest and most reliable distress signal in consumer finance, and it lands on the one party with the data, scale and cash motive to pay someone to fix it. A tenant's hospital bill is far more negotiable than a landlord's arrears, so the fix comes from the health side.
first_30_days: Recruit two ex-hospital financial counselors. Sign two mid-size operators and run 200 delinquent accounts manually via SMS and a shared inbox. Track cure rate and cost per cure. Landlords pay only after cure.

title: AltSchool Without Buildings: Disability Programs in Host Schools
one_liner: AltSchool burned $170M+ building its own schools; in Texas, the new voucher money can only reach accredited schools with two years of history, so rent that eligibility by running clinician-led disability programs inside half-empty accredited private schools.
customer: Payer: Texas families with children on IEPs holding Texas Education Freedom Accounts (about $10k standard, up to $30k for IEP students at accredited private schools). Partner: small accredited private schools, often church schools, with empty classrooms. Supply: speech-language pathologists, BCBAs and dyslexia therapists who want to run a program.
problem: TEFA rules require private schools to be accredited and to have operated two consecutive school years, and microschool or learning-pod students get only $2,000. Families holding $30k accounts cannot find seats with real special-ed capacity. Eligible incumbents have buildings but no special-ed expertise. Clinicians have expertise but no eligibility.
solution: An operating company signs a host agreement with an accredited school. The school enrolls the students as school of record and receives the TEFA funds. We supply a clinical director, staff, structured-literacy or ABA-informed curriculum, IEP compliance, the annual norm-referenced testing TEFA requires for grades 3-12, and ESA billing reconciliation. Start with 8-10 student cohorts (dyslexia and autism support). Confirm with each host's accreditor that a program-within-a-school structure is acceptable.
why_now: TEFA's first year is starting (2026-27): $1B in funding, more than 130,000 applications in the first three weeks, roughly 100,000 families expected. Texas public schools lost about 76,000 students this year and are closing dozens of campuses. Federal special-ed enforcement was hollowed out (OSEP layoffs in October 2025, with the office reportedly moving to HHS in June 2026), so parents are looking for alternatives.
revenue_model: Management fee of about 20-25% of ESA revenue per student ($6-7.5k per $30k student, so $60-75k per 10-student program per year), with a 15-20% host share; one-time program-design fee ($3-5k) per host; compliance and reconciliation SaaS later.
non_obvious_insight: AltSchool's mistake was building schools. In Texas the moat is accreditation plus a two-year operating history, which are other people's assets, so partner instead of build. Empty church-school classrooms, underemployed clinicians and $30k accounts form a three-way arbitrage that only exists because of the new rules.
first_30_days: List about 150 small accredited private schools in DFW, Houston, San Antonio and Austin using accreditor directories. Send heads of school a one-page economics sheet. Recruit 10 clinicians via LinkedIn and SLP/BCBA Facebook groups. Sign 1-2 pilot hosts for a January 2027 cohort and collect pre-enrollment interest from TEFA parent groups. First revenue is host design fees, with per-student revenue starting once enrollments transfer.

title: CPAP Off-Ramp: Retire Machines, Refurbish for Uninsured
one_liner: Re-test sleep apnea at each weight-loss milestone, help patients who have gone into remission safely come off CPAP, and refurbish the retired machines for the newly uninsured.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans and self-insured employers (paying a share of avoided rental and supply costs), cash-pay GLP-1 patients paying for the recheck, and safety-net clinics buying refurbished units.
problem: Tirzepatide is approved for moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity, and in SURMOUNT-OSA 43% to 52% of patients at the top dose met disease-resolution criteria, with apnea-hypopnea events cut by up to about 60%. Nobody is paid to notice. DME suppliers earn on continued mask and hose resupply, sleep labs earn on tests, and patients keep machines in the closet. After 13 months of Medicare rental the patient owns the machine, so it can simply be donated. Meanwhile about 4.8M people are newly uninsured after the ACA subsidy expiry, with millions more Medicaid losses due in 2027, and a $800-1,000 CPAP is out of reach.
solution: A physician-supervised pathway with a disposable home sleep apnea test at each 10% weight-loss milestone and a telehealth sleep-physician review. Patients who qualify taper or stop PAP, and are offered a buy-back credit or donation. Returned machines are sanitized, function-tested, data-wiped and re-kitted with new humidifier chambers, filters and tubing, then re-issued via licensed DME partners and clinics at roughly $150-250. Motors, foam and plastics from units that fail go to recycling.
why_now: Zepbound's OSA indication is now established and Part D can cover it. The cash-pay pill wave and the July 2026 Medicare Bridge bring far more patients on-drug. ACA and Medicaid losses create a cash-pay buyer base for cheap devices.
revenue_model: Performance fee from payers or employers of about 30% of first-year avoided rental and supply cost. Cash-pay recheck ($79-129). Margin on refurbished device sales, with a nonprofit partner able to receive donation tax deductions.
non_obvious_insight: GLP-1 success silently strands both a recurring billing stream and a physical asset. The party that finds the stranded machine can be paid twice: once by the payer for the avoided spend and once by the uninsured buyer for the second life.
first_30_days: Contract a tele-sleep physician group and a licensed DME partner. Recruit 100 patients from a cash-pay telehealth partner who have OSA and are on tirzepatide. Write the refurbishment SOP against manufacturer cleaning guidance and state DME rules. Sell the first payer or employer pilot on a savings-share basis with retrospective claims data.

title: Human Failover Retainer for Agent-Run Businesses
one_liner: Backup-generator economics for know-how: a retained, drilled bench of human operators that takes over within hours when a company's AI agents fail.
customer: Owners and COOs of 10-200 person companies that replaced back-office headcount with AI agents. First niche: freight brokerages (dispatch, carrier onboarding, load booking). Then medical billing firms, property managers, insurance agencies and 3PLs.
problem: After automation, the people who knew the manual process leave. Then a model deprecation, provider outage, prompt regression, API key ban or payment-processor freeze halts revenue, and nobody remembers how to do the job by hand. Cloud disaster-recovery plans protect servers, not the tacit process knowledge. That skill decays every month the automation succeeds.
solution: A $1.5-6k/month retainer. Phase 1: shadow the process while it still lives in staff heads and write executable runbooks and checklists. Phase 2: keep a pre-vetted bench of remote operators (ex-dispatchers, ex-billers) who sample live work weekly, so they stay current. Phase 3: run quarterly 'lights-out drills' that switch the agents off for four hours and measure time to recover. Guarantee takeover within two hours, billed hourly on activation. The bench's weekly sampling doubles as gold-label QA that flags agent drift, so the retainer also improves the agents.
why_now: 2025-26 brought large cloud and LLM-API outages (for example the October 2025 AWS us-east-1 incident), fast model deprecation cycles, and boards booking headcount cuts on the strength of agents. Insurers are starting to ask about AI-related business-interruption exposure, which gives a compliance reason to buy.
revenue_model: Monthly retainer tiered by process criticality; activation fees at $60-120 per operator-hour; drill and runbook-documentation fees; an insurer or broker referral channel that offers premium credits for a documented failover plan.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody buys a generator until the blackout, but unlike a generator the failover gets more expensive the more successful the AI rollout is, because human know-how atrophies. The best time to sell is right after a company celebrates automation savings, and the CFO can fund the retainer out of those savings. It is a services business that looks like insurance, with recurring revenue, and a bench of a few dozen part-timers can cover many clients.
first_30_days: Pick freight brokerage and find 40 brokers advertising AI dispatch or quoting. Offer a free two-hour 'lights-out drill' to about 10 of them: switch off the agents, time the recovery and hand back a one-page automation-debt score. Recruit 6 part-time ex-dispatchers as the bench. Convert 3 drill participants to $1.5-2.5k/month retainers. Package the outputs as a case study.

title: Integrity Desk for Grant Applications
one_liner: Cross-funder screening that catches AI-mass-produced applications, recycled proposals and forged partner letters before reviewers waste time.
customer: Community foundations, corporate giving programmes, state and regional economic-development agencies and accelerators, reached through grant-management platforms such as Submittable and Foundant.
problem: NIH capped principal investigators at six applications a year (effective 25 Sep 2025) after one applicant filed 40+ apparently AI-generated applications, and it says AI-developed proposals are not original work. Funders elsewhere see multiples of prior volume. Letters of support and partner commitments are the easiest thing to fabricate, and the same proposal is shopped to many funders.
solution: A plug-in and API for grant portals. It scores text reuse and AI boilerplate across applicants (including anonymised cross-funder fingerprints) and verifies claims and citations. It automatically calls back signatories of support letters for signed confirmation, checks entity registrations, tax status and beneficial owners, and keeps a shared duplicate-application registry across member funders.
why_now: LLMs drove the volume flood that prompted NIH's 2025 policy. Foundation staffing is thin, and federal and state scrutiny of grant fraud is rising.
revenue_model: $5-25k per cycle for foundations, $0.50-5 per application via portal partners, and registry membership for funders.
non_obvious_insight: This is the cURL lesson. When the cost of submission falls to zero, the reviewer's attention is the scarce resource. The winning move is not detecting AI text, which is unreliable, but verifying checkable third-party facts, like a partner's confirmation call, that AI cannot fake for free.
first_30_days: Run free pilot scans on last cycle's applications for three community foundations through regional grantmaker associations. Publish anonymised findings such as the share of applications with heavy text overlap. Pitch one grant-software vendor for a plug-in partnership.

title: Whey-Free Calf Milk Replacer
one_liner: Sell alternative-protein milk replacer to calf raisers hit by whey prices, where functionality demands are far looser than in food.
customer: Calf ranches, dairy heifer raisers, beef-on-dairy operations and regional feed mills.
problem: Calf milk replacers lean on whey protein, whose price is up 108% in two years, squeezing the operations that supply beef-on-dairy calves at the moment the herd is at a 75-year low.
solution: A milk replacer built on potato, pea, hydrolyzed and fermentation-derived proteins plus a tuned fat blend, with growth-trial performance guarantees.
why_now: Whey has become scarcer than the cheese it came from, and record calf values make feed cost per pound of gain a live issue.
revenue_model: Bag sales per pound plus per-head feeding programs with performance guarantees.
non_obvious_insight: Sell alternative proteins to animals first: feed has no clear-drink functionality bar and the buyer measures ROI in daily gain rather than taste.
first_30_days: Hire a ruminant nutritionist, run a feeding trial at two calf ranches, and offer pilot programs priced per pound of gain.

title: Chain-of-Custody Certificates for Spent PFAS Media
one_liner: A broker and tracking service that consolidates spent GAC and ion-exchange media from small utilities, routes it to verified destruction, and issues auditable certificates that document where the waste went.
customer: Small and mid-size water systems that have installed or are installing PFAS treatment, plus the treatment vendors and engineers who can bundle the service. Utilities pay per ton, and vendors pay referral fees.
problem: Step one: the 4 ppt PFOA/PFOS limits stand, monitoring is due in 2027 and compliance is proposed for 2031. Step two: treatment media saturates and must be replaced every one to three years. Step three: landfills increasingly refuse it, destruction capacity is thin, and utilities fear long-tail liability (PFOA and PFOS were designated CERCLA hazardous substances in 2024, from my background knowledge). The brief flags disposal as a downstream bottleneck but it is unverified.
solution: Start as a broker: aggregate small batches into full loads, match them to thermal reactivation, high-temperature incineration or newer destruction technologies, and issue a standard 'certificate of destruction' with custody records (tagged bulk bags, manifests, destruction-efficiency evidence and insurance). Sell it to media vendors as a bundled add-on. Later, add software for utilities' liability files.
why_now: Utilities that installed treatment after state limits and settlement money (3M and DuPont) are now hitting first change-outs. The delay from 2029 to 2031 moves the compliance date but not the disposal-liability clock.
revenue_model: 15-25% margin on disposal contracts ($ per ton), annual custody-software subscription and insurance-backed certificate fees.
non_obvious_insight: Regulatory relief changes when utilities must install treatment, not who owns the waste after it is installed. Buyers want absolution and paperwork more than the cheapest disposal, so documentation and insurance are the product.
first_30_days: Identify 10-20 utilities with early PFAS installs and imminent media change-outs from state announcements. Interview two disposal handlers and one reactivation vendor. Have an environmental attorney review a certificate template. Sign three pilot loads.

title: Dixie Flatline for Retiring Plant Operators
one_liner: Neuromancer's Dixie Flatline (a dead expert preserved as a consultable construct) built for retiring water and plant operators, with consent, clip-grounded answers and royalties paid to the expert.
customer: Municipal water and wastewater utilities, rural electric co-ops and small chemical or food plants, reached through state rural water associations and funded by state workforce and infrastructure grants.
problem: A large share of plant operators is nearing retirement, and the knowledge that matters is tacit ('when pump 3 hums like that in the cold, do this'). SOP binders miss it, experts sandbag because they fear being replaced, and a hallucinating chatbot is unacceptable when chlorine dosing is involved.
solution: A three-week Walkdown Capture: the expert tours the plant with a chest camera and mic, thinking aloud. Their answers are aligned with SCADA and alarm history so past incidents can be replayed ('what did you do in the January freeze?'). Structured critical-decision interviews feed a queryable construct that answers only with citations to the expert's own clips, deployed on a tablet or radio for night operators. The retiree signs a consent and royalty agreement, is paid per consult, can revoke, and remains reachable as a paid human escalation.
why_now: Utilities are in the middle of a retirement wave, and cheap wearable cameras, speech-to-text and retrieval systems make capture-and-query affordable for a small team. Regulators and grant programs increasingly fund workforce succession.
revenue_model: $20-45k per capture project, $1-3k per month hosting per plant, and a royalty share passed through to the expert.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not modeling but eliciting and compensating. Experts hide knowledge when the goal is replacement, and paying them a revocable royalty flips the incentive. Grounding every answer in the expert's own clips solves the hallucination problem and makes the tool defensible with regulators and insurers.
first_30_days: Ask three state rural water associations for introductions. Run one pilot with a retiring operator for $5k or free, and produce a short demo of a construct answering a night-shift question with clip evidence. Aim for three paid projects by month six.

title: Genetic-Resource Provenance Ledger for Bio-AI
one_liner: Track which genetic resources and sequences, physical and digital, feed a company's models and pipelines, so it can prove Nagoya compliance today and estimate Cali Fund exposure tomorrow.
customer: Nature-sourced discovery and AI-model builders, starting with the ABS, sustainability and legal units of large pharma, enzyme, ag, food and cosmetics groups, plus sample-collecting AI biotechs such as those mining plants and microbes.
problem: Trend chain: sequence-trained foundation models (Evo 2 trained on 9.3 trillion nucleotides across the tree of life) and proprietary sampling programs (Basecamp's Trillion Gene Atlas, Enveda's sourcing) make genetic-resource provenance a first-class asset. The Cali Fund (launched Feb 2025) asks large DSI users for roughly 1% of profits or 0.1% of revenue, but had only two contributions totaling $6,000 by August 2026. COP17 (Yerevan, Oct 19-30, 2026) is due to confirm rates and allocation. Nagoya duties for physical samples already exist, and public sequence metadata on origin is sparse. Nobody instruments any of it.
solution: Software plus advisory. Ingest sample logs and training or data manifests. Map accessions to origin metadata, flag ABS status, model Cali Fund exposure scenarios, and generate audit-ready disclosures and a 'DSI provenance statement' for model cards. Broker PIC/MAT permit packages for new sampling. Phase 1 revenue comes from existing Nagoya duties on physical collections.
why_now: COP17 is weeks away, and national DSI rules may move faster than the fund. The fund's weak uptake means the near-term product must be Nagoya and provenance assurance, with DSI as an option that COP17 could harden.
revenue_model: $25-120k annual license or advisory for enterprises, $5-15k per collection-permit package, and one-off audit sprints.
non_obvious_insight: The DSI debate is framed as a tax question, but the scarce asset is the sequence-to-origin map. If COP17 or national laws harden, whoever holds the provenance graph sells compliance to everyone. If they do not, the same graph sells 'clean provenance' assurance to acquirers and pharma partners.
first_30_days: Build a lead magnet: a 'DSI exposure snapshot' of a public training corpus or a company's sequence set. Offer 10 free snapshots to sustainability and legal leads. Recruit 2 sample-collecting AI biotechs with live ABS contracts as design partners. Partner with an ABS law firm.

title: Verified Cool-Night Rooms for Heat-Stressed Europe
one_liner: Cheap in-room sensors prove a hotel room stays below about 26C at night, sold as a certificate, a refund guarantee and a machine-readable rating for booking agents.
customer: Hotels, B&Bs and STR operators in Greece, Italy, Spain, Croatia, Portugal and Turkey, with OTAs, agent builders and insurers as secondary buyers.
problem: Summer heat makes 'air-conditioned' meaningless, since old units, weak cooling and poor insulation leave rooms hot at night. Nobody measures indoor night temperature, so complaints turn into refund disputes. Rerouted demand into Turkey and Southern Europe, and a focus on 'value for money', make heat a rising complaint.
solution: Fit a USD 10-15 wireless sensor per room in about 10 minutes. It logs a nightly indoor temperature curve, and we issue a 'Cool Night verified' certificate showing the share of nights below the threshold, with a public verification page and JSON feed for AI agents and metasearch. Hotels also get a dashboard to find and fix problem rooms, and can add a hotel-funded heat refund guarantee.
why_now: Repeated European heatwaves, cheap connected sensors, and AI booking assistants that need structured, verifiable attributes because star ratings and 'AC yes/no' are uninformative. Booking's commoditisation of listings makes measured differentiation valuable to independents.
revenue_model: EUR 6-9 per room per month, a EUR 150 install kit, an annual certification fee, and data licensing to platforms.
non_obvious_insight: Comfort is the one hotel attribute that is physically measurable yet almost never measured. In a world of agent-driven booking, a verified physical attribute becomes a ranking signal.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 hotels in Athens, Crete, Sicily and Puglia using off-the-shelf sensors. Offer a free 30-day 'truth test' and publish an anonymised heat report for press. Convert 10 to paid subscriptions.

title: Contingency Water-Bill Recovery for Small Commercial Sites
one_liner: A no-win-no-fee service that rebuilds small commercial sites' water, sewer and stormwater bills from the local tariff and claws back irrigation-sewer overcharges, leak credits and stormwater-fee errors.
customer: Owner-operators of small multi-tenant commercial properties (strip centers, 20-200 unit apartment communities, self-storage), churches, private schools and nurseries in cities that bill sewer on metered water and charge stormwater fees. Start in one drought metro. Referral partners are their bookkeepers and property managers.
problem: A $5k-$40k/yr water bill is too small for utility-audit firms, who chase national chains, and too tangled for the bookkeeper, who codes it and pays it. Tariffs sit in council resolutions. Scarcity tiers and surcharges keep changing. Sewer is often billed on metered water that includes landscape water that never reaches the sewer. Stormwater fees rest on impervious-area estimates that are often wrong. Leak-adjustment windows lapse unnoticed. The Fed's 2026 small-business survey names rising costs the #1 financial challenge.
solution: The owner forwards bills or connects QuickBooks/Xero and the utility portal. An LLM pipeline reads the tariff PDF and rebuilds every bill. It flags misclassified meters, irrigation on sewered meters, overnight-flow leak periods in interval data, impervious-area disputes (checked against aerial imagery) and estimated reads. A human analyst files the credit, refund or reclassification with the utility, chases it to cash, and writes corrected coding back into the books. Wedge product: an 'irrigation-sewer plus stormwater credit audit' for one metro and three utilities.
why_now: 49.6% of the US was in drought on Sept 24, 2026 after the warmest June-August on record, so scarcity pricing and surcharges are multiplying. Regulated private water companies invested about $6.8B in 2025 ($43.5B over the decade) and recover it through rate cases that small customers never see. LLMs make it cheap to read hundreds of heterogeneous tariffs and bills. Customer portals increasingly expose interval meter data. Intuit and Xero are rebuilding around LLM subscriptions and cannot easily take contingency fees.
revenue_model: 30% of verified first-year savings plus recovered refunds (contingency). Then a $25/site/month monitoring plan that stops corrections regressing and catches new leak periods. White-label for property managers at about $8/door/year.
non_obvious_insight: The one-time refund is the hook, not the product. The value is the permanent reclassification of the account (meter class, irrigation split, impervious area), which lowers every future bill. The moat is a tariff library that human auditors cannot afford to build for accounts this small. Outcome-priced work does not fit subscription incumbents, so the real competitor is nobody.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with a published stormwater-credit manual and an irrigation or deduct-meter option. Hand-collect five utilities' tariffs. Recruit 20 owners through the local apartment association or BOMA chapter and 5 bookkeepers who get a 10% referral. Audit 24 months of bills per site with the LLM pipeline plus one analyst, with no upfront fee. Targets: 10 audits by day 30, first 3 recovered checks by day 60, then publish anonymized results as the sales asset.

title: Camera-Free Nap-Room Proof-of-Supervision
one_liner: Start with NFC crib tags that create tamper-evident safe-sleep check logs for childcare centers, then add 60GHz radar that verifies presence and breathing without any camera.
customer: Childcare centers' infant and toddler rooms, small chains, childcare liability insurers and brokers, and licensing agencies.
problem: Safe-sleep checks are handwritten logs that can be filled in after the fact. Sleep supervision failures drive licensing violations, insurance claims and tragedies. Cameras raise privacy objections. After abuse incidents at premium chains (Bright Horizons NYC, per the brief), parents and insurers want proof that supervision happened, not just cameras.
solution: Phase 1: teachers tap a badge on an NFC tag at each crib every interval, producing a timestamped, tamper-evident log and alerts for missed checks. Phase 2: a ceiling-mounted mmWave radar puck detects presence, motion and position class with no images, cross-checking the log. Positioned as compliance logging, not a medical device.
why_now: Low-cost 60GHz radar chips and infant-sensing research are now mature. Insurers are tightening abuse and molestation coverage (from memory). Public attention to childcare safety is high after the 2025-26 incidents.
revenue_model: $20-45 per crib per month plus a $150 radar device, with insurer premium-credit revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The value is proof of supervision, not detection. Detection claims invite FDA regulation and false-assurance liability, while insurers and inspectors will pay for un-fakeable evidence that checks happened.
first_30_days: Build the NFC tag and phone app. Pilot in 3 infant rooms. Talk to 2 childcare insurers or brokers about premium credits. Prototype breathing detection on an evaluation radar board with adult volunteers and a manikin, never infants.

title: Crop Scouts of the Sea for Seafood Buyers
one_liner: A paid panel of working skippers and tender operators that texts in daily run, quality and delivery-limit data, sold to seafood buyers and lenders days to weeks before the market sees it.
customer: Wild-salmon importers and distributors, club-store and retail category buyers, Japanese and European trading houses, canned and frozen sockeye brokers, banks lending to processors, reinsurers and commodity funds. Each pays $10-30K/year. Panelists are paid, so fishermen are also customers of the cash flow.
problem: Bristol Bay is the source of most of the world's wild sockeye, and price went from $1.03/lb avg in 2025 (41.2M fish) to $1.72/lb in 2026 (30.1M fish). Farmed Atlantic salmon has futures and analyst coverage. Wild sockeye has neither. Buyers see ADF&G escapement and harvest counts and press releases, but not fish size, color, quality, roe, which processors are on delivery limits, tender backlogs, or which plants are paying up for fish. That information reaches the market 2-4 weeks late, after forward prices are already set.
solution: Recruit 150-300 skippers, crew and tender operators. Each sends a 60-second daily check-in (pounds per boat, average fish weight, limit status by processor, hours waiting at the tender, water temp, color and quality, weather, gear). Validate it against ADF&G counts and AIS. Publish a daily 'Fisher's Report' with the run-timing curve, quality and limit maps, and proprietary indexes, plus a weekly call with a retired skipper as analyst. Extend to Copper River, Prince William Sound, Kodiak and Southeast.
why_now: The one-year 67% swing in average price has made buyers and lenders hungry for earlier signals. Alt-data buyers already pay for crop scouts and satellite counts in other commodities. Starlink on boats makes real-time reporting possible. LLMs can clean messy text reports into structured data at almost no cost.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $12-30K/year per company, custom data feeds at $50K+, and analyst calls. Pay panelists $150-400 per season out of 20-30% of revenue. Add other fisheries and other 'boots on the ground' sectors later.
non_obvious_insight: Information in the fleet moves at VHF speed. The whole fleet knows the run is late, the fish are small, or the tenders are backed up days before any official number, and buyers treat it as noise. Skippers will happily share anonymized volume and quality data if you pay them, because it does not touch their contract terms or fishing spots. The valuable part is aggregation and a track record. Keep panelists' data separate from any confidential processor contract terms, and get securities and antitrust counsel before selling to funds.
first_30_days: Recruit 40 panelists from Facebook groups and associations while everyone is idle after settlements. Ask them for 2026 season logs (many keep daily notes and fish tickets). Backtest against ADF&G data and the 2026 price path, and show the panel's signals would have led the market. Send a sample '2026 in hindsight' report to 30 importers and analysts. Aim for 3 pilot subscriptions at about $5K each before the May opener.

title: Dog Walkers as Repeat-Pass Sidewalk Inspectors
one_liner: Pay dog walkers a few dollars a day to mount a phone on their chest and sell the resulting block-by-block sidewalk condition layer to cities, utilities, and delivery-robot operators.
customer: City public works and ADA coordinators (mid-size cities of 100k to 500k people first), plus fiber and utility contractors and sidewalk delivery-robot operators as second buyers. Walkers are the paid supply side.
problem: Cities are legally on the hook to inventory sidewalks and curb ramps and fix trip hazards. Today that means an expensive contractor van or LiDAR survey every 5 to 10 years, or 311 complaints that skew toward loud, wealthy neighborhoods. Residential side streets go stale, and nobody sees a slab heave, a missing curb ramp, or a new obstruction until someone sues or gets hurt.
solution: A harness or chest mount plus a background app that runs during walks. It records geotagged video, and an on-device model flags heaved slabs, missing or noncompliant curb ramps, obstructions, standing water, and broken glass. Faces and plates are blurred on the phone and nothing is recorded near windows or interiors. Walkers earn per validated mile (roughly $1 a mile, so about $8 to $15 a day for something they already do). The city gets a rolling map with change detection, exported to its existing GIS or asset-management tools. A free 'dog hazard' layer (glass, bait or poison reports, hot pavement, off-leash aggressive dogs) gives walkers and owners a reason to adopt it. I have not verified current competitors or municipal pricing, so both should be checked before the pitch.
why_now: In 2026 a phone can run a decent defect-detection model offline, which was not practical a few years ago. Cities face ongoing ADA sidewalk obligations and litigation risk with tight budgets, which favors cheap continuous data over big one-off surveys. Driver-sourced street imagery (Hivemapper and Nexar style) has proven that crowds get paid for mapping, but the pedestrian tier is essentially unclaimed.
revenue_model: Annual municipal data subscription, or per-mile survey pricing that undercuts contractor quotes, at roughly $20k to $150k a year per city. Secondary sales of the same data to utilities, telecom build QA, and robot-delivery mapping. Walkers are paid about 30 to 40 percent of revenue as per-mile payouts.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody walks a residential sidewalk more than a dog walker: the same 3 to 5 miles, five days a week, at a slow pace, with eyes on the ground because dogs eat everything. The scarce asset in infrastructure data is not coverage, it is repeat passes, which is what makes change detection possible. That is exactly what a walker's fixed route produces for free.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 to 20 walkers through local pet-sitter Facebook groups and Nextdoor, since they are already clustered by neighborhood. Build the capture app with a cheap phone mount and an open sidewalk-defect model fine-tuned on public sidewalk datasets. Map about 200 miles of one neighborhood, then take a before-and-after sample to a city ADA or transportation coordinator. Offer a free neighborhood pilot with a cost comparison against contractor rates, and aim for a small pilot purchase order under the city's simple-purchase threshold.
